title: Constructors
relevance: Constructors are a core C++ OOP check in SDE interviews and OAs—initialization rules, copy semantics, and resource ownership trip up candidates constantly.

phases.goal: Establish what a constructor is and the kinds a class can have.

must_hit.point: A constructor is a special member function that runs automatically when an object is created to initialise the object's data; it has the same name as the class and no return type (not even void).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names same-as-class, no return type, runs on object creation for initialization.

must_hit.point: The four kinds are default (compiler-supplied when none written), non-parameterised (user-written, no args), parameterised (takes args), and copy (builds from an existing object).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists default vs non-parameterised vs parameterised vs copy with the Rectangle examples.

must_hit.point: Constructors are overloaded by parameter lists; default arguments can collapse the non-parameterised and parameterised versions into one constructor.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions overload by parameter list and Rectangle(int l = 0, int b = 0) serving both call forms.

probes: What is a constructor, and what kinds can a C++ class have?

hints.1: Think about what runs when you write Rectangle r1; versus Rectangle r2(10, 5); versus Rectangle r3(r2).
hints.2: Cover same-name/no-return-type, then default, non-parameterised, parameterised, and copy.
hints.3: A constructor initialises on creation; compiler default leaves members uninitialised or value-initialised; you can overload or use defaults like Rectangle(int l = 0, int b = 0).

phases.goal: Explain how constructors initialise members and how C++11 controls generation and conversions.

must_hit.point: The member initialiser list (after the parameter list and a colon) does single-step direct initialisation; body assignment is two-step: default-construct then assign.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts : length(l), breadth(b) with assignment in the body and names the two-step vs one-step difference.

must_hit.point: const members, reference members, and base class subobjects without a default constructor must be initialised via the member initialiser list.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists exactly those three cases that cannot be assigned after creation.

must_hit.point: Members in the initialiser list are initialised in class declaration order, not the order written in the list.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says length is still initialised first even if the list writes breadth before length.

must_hit.point: C++11 NSDMI sets in-class defaults; an initialiser list overrides them; delegating constructors call another constructor of the same class via the initialiser list; = default requests the compiler version and = delete forbids a constructor; a single-argument constructor is an implicit conversion unless marked explicit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers NSDMI, delegation like Rectangle() : Rectangle(1, 1), = default/= delete, and explicit blocking printString(50).

probes: Why prefer the member initialiser list over assignment in the body, and what else can constructors do in modern C++?

hints.1: Start with how members get their first value—list versus body.
hints.2: Then name what must use the list, declaration-order rule, NSDMI, delegation, explicit, and = default/= delete.
hints.3: List is more efficient for object members and mandatory for const, references, and non-default-constructible bases; declaration order wins; explicit stops silent conversions.

phases.goal: Weigh initialisation styles and copy strategies the file contrasts.

must_hit.point: For primitive types like int the performance difference between body assignment and the initialiser list is negligible; for complex object members the list avoids a wasted default construction.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States negligible cost for int and wasted default construction for complex members.

must_hit.point: Compiler default copy is member-as-is (shallow for pointers—both objects share one heap block); a deep copy allocates a fresh block and copies contents so each object owns an independent array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts p = t.p with new int[a] plus element copy, and why pointer-owning classes need deep copy.

must_hit.point: NSDMI reduces boilerplate across constructors and prevents uninitialised members if a constructor forgets a member; the initialiser list still overrides those defaults when provided.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties in-class defaults to less forgetting/boilerplate and list override.

probes: When is the member initialiser list worth it versus body assignment, and when is shallow copy wrong?

hints.1: Compare cheap ints to members that are objects or owning pointers.
hints.2: Separately contrast default memberwise copy with allocating your own array in the copy constructor.
hints.3: Prefer the list for complex members and required cases; deep-copy pointer-owned resources so destroy/modify of one does not corrupt the other.

phases.goal: Apply constructor rules to safe APIs and owning types.

must_hit.point: Mark a single-argument constructor explicit when silent conversions are dangerous, so call sites must construct explicitly (e.g. String(50)) instead of passing a raw int.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses the String(int size) / printString(50) story and explicit making the implicit call a compiler error.

must_hit.point: Whenever a class manages a resource through a pointer, its copy constructor must perform a deep copy so objects are not entangled and both do not try to manage one block.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the owning-pointer rule and the Test deep-copy pattern with a separate array.

must_hit.point: Use = default for the compiler-generated default constructor and = delete on the copy constructor to forbid copying (NonCopyable pattern).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites NonCopyable() = default and NonCopyable(const NonCopyable&) = delete.

probes: How would you stop implicit conversions from a single-arg constructor, and how should a class that owns a heap array copy?

hints.1: Think about String taking an int size and a class with an int* to a new[] buffer.
hints.2: One knob is explicit; the other is deep copy or deleting copy.
hints.3: explicit String(int); deep copy with new int[a] and element copy, or = delete the copy constructor for non-copyable types.

tradeoffs.topic: Member initialiser list vs assignment in the constructor body
tradeoffs.strong_answer: The list is single-step direct initialisation; body assignment default-constructs then assigns. Prefer the list for complex object members (avoids wasted default construction) and whenever const, reference, or non-default-constructible base members require it; for int the cost difference is negligible.

Default/memberwise copy of a pointer is shallow—both objects share one heap block and become entangled. Deep copy allocates a fresh block and copies elements so each object owns an independent array; required when the class manages a resource through a pointer.

tradeoffs.topic: Separate no-arg constructor vs one constructor with default arguments
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Default arguments can collapse non-parameterised and parameterised into one, but providing both Rectangle(int l = 0, int b = 0) and Rectangle() makes Rectangle r; ambiguous.

gotchas.trap: Providing both a constructor with all-default arguments and a separate no-argument constructor.
gotchas.correction: The compiler reports ambiguity on Rectangle r; because both are valid matches—keep only one of those forms.

gotchas.trap: Assuming initialiser-list order is the order written in the list.
gotchas.correction: Members initialise in declaration order in the class; match the list to declaration order so dependent initialisations are not wrong.
It acts as an implicit conversion (e.g. printString(50) becomes String(50)); mark it explicit so only explicit construction compiles.

gotchas.trap: Relying on the compiler copy constructor when a member is an owning pointer.
gotchas.correction: That is a shallow copy (p = t.p); implement a deep copy that allocates and copies the array, or delete copying if the type should not be copied.
